title: Are Car Extended Warranties a Scam?
summary: A Toyota/Lexus technician explains when an extended warranty makes sense (long-term ownership, used cars), red flags (lifetime claims, uninspected online sellers), and how to negotiate price.

assertions.quote: this is the person that a sender warranty may make sense to because it could not be something big

verdicts.note: Directionally sound, but benefit still depends on the vehicle's actual failure rate and the plan's price and exclusions.

assertions.quote: you don't know how the previous owner took care of it

verdicts.note: A reasonable argument, but a pre-purchase inspection and vehicle history report address much of the same uncertainty more cheaply.

assertions.quote: Lifetime warranties are too good to be true because they are too good to be true

verdicts.note: Most 'lifetime' plans redefine the term with mileage or year caps in the fine print, though a few genuine long-term manufacturer plans exist.

assertions.quote: it is a big mistake to roll your taxes and your extended warranty into the loan

verdicts.note: Straightforward interest-cost math, confirmed by Consumer Reports' reporting on the practice.

assertions.quote: Negotiate the price of the extended warranty. They will lock initially tell you, No, it's not the warranty

verdicts.note: Consumer Reports found most buyers who tried to negotiate succeeded, saving money on average.

assertions.quote: most of the good extended warranty companies do not sell you to the consumer directly because they want the car inspected

verdicts.note: Described by an industry source as standard practice among reputable providers.

assertions.quote: be very wary of extended warranties that are sold online

verdicts.note: A plausible claim from an industry insider, but not independently verified against actual claim outcomes by provider type.
